Comprehension – C1 Answer the following questions and share your answers with your partner. Then write. (p. 6)
1. Who was Vasishta?
Vasishta was a sage (a wise hermit) who lived in a forest.
2. Where did he live?
He lived in a forest.
3. What was special about Shabale?
Shabale could give Vasishta whatever he asked for, such as food, drink or clothes.
4. What did Kaushika ask Vasishta?
Kaushika asked Vasishta to give Shabale to him in exchange for ten thousand cows. He even offered his entire kingdom.
5. What did Kaushika realize?
Kaushika realized that he was not powerful enough and could not win anything by force.

Answer “Yes” or “No” in a full sentence: Was Shabale an ordinary cow?
qb.a: No, Shabale was not an ordinary cow.

qb.q: Answer “Yes” or “No” in a full sentence: Did King Kaushika want Shabale for himself?
qb.a: Yes, King Kaushika wanted Shabale for himself.

qb.q: Answer “Yes” or “No” in a full sentence: Did Shabale create an army using her divine powers?

qb.q: Answer “Yes” or “No” in a full sentence: Does the story show the result of greed and pride?
qb.a: Yes, the story shows the result of greed and pride.

qb.q: Who was Shabale?
qb.a: Shabale was the sage Vasishtha's divine cow.

qb.q: Where did sage Vasishtha live?
qb.a: He lived in a peaceful ashram with his disciples.

qb.q: Why did King Kaushika visit the sage?
qb.a: He came to rest at the sage's ashram during a journey.

qb.q: What did the king want from the sage?
qb.a: The king wanted to take Shabale with him.

qb.q: Did the sage agree to give Shabale to the king? Why or why not?
qb.a: No, the sage refused because Shabale was a gift from the gods and very special to him.

qb.q: What happened when the king's soldiers tried to take Shabale?
qb.a: Shabale used her divine powers and defeated the king's soldiers.

qb.q: How did Shabale protect the sage and herself?
qb.a: She created powerful warriors with her powers and stopped the king's army.

qb.q: What did King Kaushika decide to do after his defeat?
qb.a: He decided to give up fighting and become a sage.

qb.q: What lesson do you learn from this story?
qb.a: We learn that spiritual power is stronger than physical strength and greed leads to failure.

qb.q: Who said this to whom? 'Give me your cow.'
qb.a: King Kaushika said this to sage Vasishta.

qb.q: Who said this to whom? 'I will not give away Shabale.'

qb.q: Who said this to whom? 'Give me food, clothes and drinks, O divine cow!'
qb.a: Sage Vasishta said this to Shabale.

qb.q: Write about the changes Shabale underwent to save herself.
qb.a: When King Kaushika's soldiers tried to take her by force, Shabale used her divine powers. She changed her form by creating strong warriors from her body. These warriors fought the soldiers and protected her. This change showed that she was not an ordinary cow but a powerful divine being.

qb.q: How did Shabale teach a lesson to Kaushika?
qb.a: Kaushika wanted to take Shabale without understanding her true value. When he tried to use force, Shabale used her powers and defeated his army. This surprised and humbled Kaushika. He realised that spiritual strength is more powerful than weapons and became a sage to learn wisdom.

qb.q: Look at the picture and write four dialogues between King Kaushika and Sage Vasishtha. (ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಚಿತ್ರ ಇನ್ನೂ ಸೇರಿಸಿಲ್ಲ, ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ)
qb.a: King Kaushika: 'Sage Vasishtha, I am amazed by this cow. I want to take her to my palace.' / Sage Vasishtha: 'O King, Shabale is not an ordinary cow. She is a divine gift and cannot be given away.' / King Kaushika: 'But I am the king! I can use her powers for my kingdom. I must have her.' / Sage Vasishtha: 'Power is not everything, O King. You must understand her value before trying to take her by force.'

qb.q: Complete the story in proper sentences using the clues: Shabale the heavenly cow – gift to sage Vasishta – kind, magical – Kaushika wanted her by force – she fights and protects herself – Kaushika leaves.
qb.a: Shabale was a heavenly cow gifted to sage Vasishtha by the gods. She was kind and had magical powers. One day, King Kaushika came to the ashram and wanted to take Shabale by force. But Shabale used her powers to fight back and protect herself. Kaushika was shocked and realised his mistake. He left the ashram quietly, having learned a lesson.

Comprehension – C1 Answer the following questions and share your answers with your partner. Then write. (p. 19)
1. What kind of a boy was the businessman's son?
He was a lazy boy. He was not used to doing any kind of work.
2. What did the businessman tell his son?
He told his son to go out and earn something; otherwise he would not be given food tonight.
3. Why did the mother give her son a gold coin?
Her heart melted at the sight of tears in her son's eyes.
4. What did the father ask the son to do with the coins?
He asked his son to throw the coins into the well in front of their house.
5. Why did the son go to the market?
He went to the market in search of work, because no one was there to help him this time and his father wanted him to earn something.
6. How did he earn two rupees?
He earned two rupees by carrying a shopkeeper's bag to his house.
7. Why was the boy not ready to throw the two-rupee coin into the well?
Because he had earned it through hard work. His whole body was aching, his feet were trembling and his palms had rashes.
Comprehension – C2 Discuss with your friends and answer the following questions in four to six sentences each. (p. 19)
1. Describe the attitude of the boy towards work.

ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: At first the boy was lazy and did not want to work; he was not used to any kind of work. After he earned two rupees by carrying a shopkeeper's bag, he understood the value of hard work. He realised the value of labour and promised never to be lazy again.
2. Explain the feelings of the boy when he said, '... you are asking me to throw my hard-earned money into the well!'

ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: The boy was hurt and upset. He had worked very hard, his whole body was aching and his palms had rashes. He felt it was unfair to throw the money he had earned into the well, so he cried out in pain and told his father that it was his hard-earned money.

qb.q: Why did the businessman want his son to earn something on his own?
qb.a: He wanted his son to be hard-working and responsible, and to realise the value of labour.

qb.q: How did the boy get the gold coin on the first day?
qb.a: The boy cried to his mother, and she gave him a gold coin because she felt sorry for him.

qb.q: What did the father do when he realised someone else was helping the boy?
qb.a: He sent his daughter back to her in-law's house, so that no one could help the boy and he would be forced to earn on his own. (ಪುಸ್ತಕದ ಕೀ 'wife and daughter' ಎಂದಿತ್ತು; ಪಠ್ಯದ ಪ್ರಕಾರ 'daughter' ಮಾತ್ರ.)

qb.q: Describe the boy's condition after he earned two rupees by working.
qb.a: He was sweating, his feet were trembling, his neck and back were aching, and his palms had rashes.

qb.q: How did the boy react when asked to throw his hard-earned money into the well?
qb.a: He cried out in pain, saying he had worked hard for the money and did not want to throw it away.

qb.q: What lesson did the boy learn by the end of the story?
qb.a: He learned the value of hard work and promised never to be lazy again.

qb.q: Why did the father ask his son to throw the coin into the well each time?
qb.a: To test whether the money had been earned through hard work; if it was, the boy would hesitate to throw it away.

qb.q: What did the father do after the boy realised the value of labour?
qb.a: He was happy and handed over the keys of his shop to the boy, trusting him with responsibility.

qb.q: Look at the picture. What do you see? What do you think the boy is feeling? Use 3–4 sentences. (ಚಿತ್ರ ಆಧಾರಿತ – ಚಿತ್ರ ಇನ್ನೂ ಸೇರಿಸಿಲ್ಲ, ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ)
qb.a: I see a boy carrying a heavy bag. He looks very tired and is sweating. His face shows that he is in pain. I think he has been working hard to earn money.

qb.q: What did the boy learn at the end of the story?
qb.a: The boy learned that it is important to work hard. He felt proud after earning money himself. He understood that money should not be wasted. He promised his father that he would never be lazy again.

qb.q: Write 4 sentences about the father in the story.
qb.a: The father was a rich businessman. He wanted his son to learn the value of hard work. He tested his son by asking him to throw money into the well. In the end, he was happy and gave the shop keys to his son.

qb.q: Complete the story using the clues: father, lazy, gold coin, well, hard work, shop.
qb.a: There was a rich businessman who had a lazy son. The son did not want to work. One day, the father asked him to earn money. First, the mother gave him a gold coin. The father told him to throw it into the well. Later, the boy did real work and earned money by carrying a bag to a shop.

qb.q: Who was the lazy son's father in the story?
What did the mother do when her son cried?
qb.a: She gave him a gold coin because she felt sorry for him.

qb.q: Why did the father send his daughter back to her in-law's house?
qb.a: So that she would not help the boy again. (ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ತಿದ್ದುಪಡಿ: ಪುಸ್ತಕದಲ್ಲಿ 'mother' ಎಂದಿತ್ತು; ಕಥೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಮಗಳು.)

qb.q: Who gave the boy a rupee coin on the second day? What was her relationship to him?
qb.a: His sister gave him a rupee coin. She was his sister.

qb.q: What did the father do when he saw his son had learned the value of hard work?
qb.a: He handed over the keys of his shop to his son.

qb.q: List two kinship words from the story and make your own sentences with them.
qb.a: Father – My father teaches me the value of hard work. Sister – My sister helps me with my homework every evening. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಸ್ವಂತ ವಾಕ್ಯಗಳು ಬೇರೆಯಾಗಿರಬಹುದು.)

lessons.t: Unit 7 · A Great Coachman (ಒಬ್ಬ ಮಹಾನ್ ಕೋಚ್‌ಮನ್) · Paper Boats (ಕಾಗದದ ಹಡಗುಗಳು)
lessons.words: coach – horse-drawn carriage; desire – wish; scholar – a learned person; wandering – moving from place to place; monk – a holy man; social evils – evils that affect the society (ಸಾಮಾಜಿಕ ಪಿಡುಗುಗಳು); caste system – different groups in the society; superstitions – blind faith (ಮೂಢನಂಬಿಕೆಗಳು); religions – systems of faith and worship; brotherhood – a feeling that all belong to a family and are brothers and sisters (ಸೋದರಭಾವ); motto – that expresses the aims and beliefs of a person (ಧ್ಯೇಯವಾಕ್ಯ); achievements – great works; stream – flowing water; strange – unknown; shiuli flowers – white and orange parijatha flowers; blooms – bud opening into flower; dawn – time of first sunshine; launch – send; bulging – swollen; playmate – a friend; fairies – beautiful, charming ladies who live in the other world; lading – load
lessons.notes: Unit 7 has a prose lesson (A Great Coachman, p. 23–29) with Prepositions grammar, a poem (Paper Boats, p. 30–31) and an activity page (p. 33). Competency: Prepositions.
ab: Warm-up Activity – Task 1: What do you want to be when you grow up? Why do you want to become thus? Discuss with your friends. (p. 23)
What do you want to be when you grow up? Why?
ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: I want to be a teacher, because I like helping children learn new things. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಸ್ವಂತ ಉತ್ತರ ಬೇರೆಯಾಗಿರಬಹುದು.)
Warm-up Activity – Task 2: A. Name some of your family members whom you think are great. B. Name some great men of our country. (p. 23)
A. Name some of your family members whom you think are great.
ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: My grandfather, my mother and my father. (ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಸ್ವಂತ ಉತ್ತರ ಬೇರೆಯಾಗಿರಬಹುದು.)
B. Name some great men of our country.
ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: Swami Vivekananda; Mahatma Gandhi; Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. (ಪಠ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಸ್ವಾಮಿ ವಿವೇಕಾನಂದರ ಹೆಸರು ಇದೆ.)

Comprehension – C1 Answer the following questions in two to three sentences each. (p. 27)
1. What did Naren tell his mother one day?
Naren told his mother that he wanted to be a coachman like the coachman he had seen, because it was so nice to drive a coach.
2. What picture did the mother show him?

(ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ – ಪಠ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ತಾಯಿ 'ಚಿತ್ರ' ತೋರಿಸಿದ ಉಲ್ಲೇಖವಿಲ್ಲ. ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆಯನ್ನು 'What did the mother tell him?' ಎಂದು ತಿದ್ದುಪಡಿ ಮಾಡಬಹುದು.) ಸರಿಯಾದ ಉತ್ತರ (ತಿದ್ದುಪಡಿ ನಂತರ): She told him that he should be a coachman like Krishna, who guided Arjuna and showed the path to the innocent people of the universe.
3. When was Naren born?
Naren was born on 12th January 1863.
4. Who was Narendranath's guru?
Ramakrishna Paramahamsa was Narendranath's guru.
5. What is the motto of Ramakrishna Mission?
The main motto of Ramakrishna Mission is 'Work is Worship'.
Comprehension – C2 Discuss in groups and answer the following questions in five to six sentences each. (p. 27)
1. '...you should be a coachman like Krishna.' What did Naren's mother mean?

ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: She meant that Naren should be a guide who shows people the right path in life, as Krishna guided Arjuna and showed the path to the innocent people of the universe. Naren could not understand this clearly at that time, but later he became Swami Vivekananda, who guided people through his teachings.
2. What did Vivekananda tell in the Parliament of World Religions at Chicago?
He said that all religions in the world preached the same truth. Therefore everyone should develop a sense of brotherhood and love each other.
3. Collect pictures of Swami Vivekananda and write about Swami Vivekananda's life.

ಮಾದರಿ ಉತ್ತರ: Swami Vivekananda was born on 12 January 1863 to Vishwanath Dutta and Bhuvaneshwari Devi and was named Narendranath Dutta. He met his guru Ramakrishna Paramahamsa. In 1893 he gave a great speech at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago. He founded Belur Math in Calcutta. He lived for only 39 years. (ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಚಿತ್ರಗಳನ್ನು ಸಂಗ್ರಹಿಸಿ ತಮ್ಮದೇ ಮಾತುಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಬರೆಯಬೇಕು.)

Poetry – Paper Boats · Comprehension – C1 Answer the following questions in two to three sentences each. (p. 32)
1. How many boats did the child float?
The poem does not give an exact number. The child floats many paper boats, one by one, day by day. (ಪರಿಶೀಲಿಸಿ – ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ಸ್ಪಷ್ಟತೆ.)
2. Why did the child write its name on the boat?
The child wrote the name of himself/herself and the name of the village on the boats, so that someone in some strange land who finds them would know who the child is.
3. What did the child load the boat with?
The child loaded the little boats with shiuli flowers from the garden.
4. What did the child dream at night?
The child dreamt that the paper boats float on and on under the midnight stars.

qb.q: What did Swami Vivekananda do after returning to India?

qb.q: What did Swami Vivekananda believe about all religions?
qb.a: He believed that all religions teach the same essential truth and should lead to unity, not division.

qb.q: What inspired Naren to seek spiritual knowledge?

qb.q: Describe Swami Vivekananda's life as a monk.
qb.a: He became a wandering monk, travelling across India to spread awareness about spirituality, education and social reform.

qb.q: What was the goal of Swami Vivekananda's speeches?
qb.a: To awaken the spirit of India, promote religious harmony and fight against social evils.

qb.q: How did Swami Vivekananda inspire youth?
qb.a: He motivated them to be strong, fearless and committed to national and personal development through education and service.

qb.q: What was the main idea behind Vivekananda's message at Chicago?
qb.a: He stressed that all religions are paths to the same truth and promoted universal brotherhood.

qb.q: Why is the year 1893 important in Swami Vivekananda's life?
qb.a: It was the year he addressed the Parliament of Religions in Chicago and gained international fame.

qb.q: What did Vivekananda say about work in relation to worship?
qb.a: He believed “Work is Worship”, meaning that serving humanity is equivalent to serving God.

qb.q: What is the importance of Belur Math?
qb.a: It is the centre of the Ramakrishna Mission, which promotes service and education.

Write a short essay on the childhood of Swami Vivekananda.
qb.a: Narendranath Dutta, later Swami Vivekananda, was born on 12th January 1863. He was the son of Vishwanath Dutta and Bhuvaneshwari Devi. From an early age he was interested in spirituality, mythology and philosophy, and was influenced by the Ramayana and Mahabharata. He was a curious and bright student, and his desire to see God marked the beginning of his spiritual journey. (ಜನ್ಮಸ್ಥಳ ಪಠ್ಯದಲ್ಲಿ ಇಲ್ಲ; ಉತ್ತರದಿಂದ ತೆಗೆಯಲಾಗಿದೆ.)

qb.q: Describe Swami Vivekananda's contribution to Indian society.
qb.a: He worked for education that develops the complete human being, fought against social evils like the caste system and superstitions, and encouraged youth to be strong and self-reliant. Through his speeches and writings he spread universal brotherhood and religious tolerance. His speech at the Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893 placed India on the world stage.

qb.q: Write a short paragraph on the teachings of Swami Vivekananda.
qb.a: Vivekananda taught self-reliance, the pursuit of knowledge and the realisation of one's inner strength. He believed education should develop not only the mind but also character. He emphasised the unity of all religions and preached universal love, tolerance and respect. He said true spirituality lies in the service of humanity.

qb.q: Write about the significance of Belur Math and its motto.
qb.a: Belur Math in Calcutta is the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission, founded by Swami Vivekananda. It symbolises his vision of spiritual unity and service. Its motto, “Work is Worship”, means that serving humanity is the highest form of devotion to God.

qb.q: Write a note on the relationship between Swami Vivekananda and his guru Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.
qb.a: Ramakrishna recognised Narendra's potential and guided him on his spiritual journey. Under his guidance Vivekananda had deep spiritual experiences and became committed to serving humanity. Vivekananda regarded Ramakrishna as his divine guide.

qb.q: Continue the story: “Little Naren wanted to be a coachman...” and end it with how he became Swami Vivekananda.
qb.a: Little Naren wanted to be a coachman because he thought it would be thrilling to drive the coach. His mother said, “If you wish to be a coachman, be like Krishna, who guided Arjuna and led people to the right path.” As he grew, Naren sought the deeper meaning of life, met Ramakrishna Paramahamsa and later travelled across India. He became Swami Vivekananda, who showed the world how to live with purpose and love for humanity.

qb.q: Write a character sketch of Narendra as a child.
qb.a: Narendra (later Swami Vivekananda) was an inquisitive and intelligent child with a deep interest in philosophy, religion and spirituality. He was curious about the world and often questioned society's norms. He had a desire to understand the deeper truths of life and was known for his sincerity and sense of justice.

qb.q: Describe Swami Vivekananda as a leader and reformer.
qb.a: Swami Vivekananda was a spiritual leader, social reformer and philosopher. He advocated education that develops the mind and character, fought against social evils, encouraged youth to realise their potential, and inspired people to serve humanity selflessly. His teachings continue to inspire generations.

qb.q: What can today's youth learn from Swami Vivekananda's life?
qb.a: Today's youth can learn self-discipline, the pursuit of knowledge and the value of social service. He taught that true education should cultivate character, self-reliance and compassion, and he inspired young people to rise above personal struggles and serve society.

qb.q: Discuss the themes of childhood innocence and imagination in Tagore's poem 'Paper Boats'.
qb.a: In 'Paper Boats', Tagore captures a child's simple act of floating paper boats down a stream. The child writes his name and village on them, loads them with shiuli flowers, and imagines clouds as sails racing with his boats and fairies of sleep carrying dreams. These images show childhood innocence and a rich imagination that turns ordinary things into a magical world.

qb.q: Write a short composition on the joy of making paper boats.

qb.q: Why does the poet consider dying for his country as a divine lot?
qb.a: He sees dying for his country as a noble sacrifice and an honourable fate, a divine lot.

qb.q: What role do the women play in the poet's description of the land?
qb.a: The poet praises the women for their steadfastness; their hearts never waver.

qb.q: How does the poet view the men of his land?
qb.a: The poet believes no men are braver than the men of his homeland.

qb.q: What is the central theme of the poem?
qb.a: The central theme is patriotism and deep love for one's homeland.

qb.q: How does the poet feel about the land's beauty?
qb.a: He feels deep pride in the land and describes it as fair, rare and fresh.

qb.q: Explain the poet's love and pride for his native land.
qb.a: In “My Land” the poet expresses deep love and pride for his homeland. He praises it as rich, rare, warm and bold, and admires the bravery of its men, who are braver than all others. The women's hearts never waver. He would freely die to save the land and considers such a fate divine, so his love for the land is strong and sincere.

qb.q: Discuss the poet's description of the land's people in the poem.
qb.a: The poet describes the people of his land with admiration. He praises the bravery of the men, saying no men are braver than those of his homeland. The women are praised for their steadfastness, since their hearts never waver. Both men and women are shown as noble and loyal.

qb.q: What does the poet mean by “freely die” for his country? Discuss the significance of this idea.
qb.a: When the poet says he would “freely die” for his country, he means he would give his life willingly and without hesitation. This shows his patriotism and loyalty. He calls his lot divine, which means he sees such a sacrifice as honourable and sacred.

qb.q: Discuss the poet's perspective on sacrifice and patriotism in the poem.
qb.a: The poet views patriotism as deep love and devotion to one's country. He believes a true patriot is willing to sacrifice even life for the homeland. He considers such a death noble and divine, which shows his unwavering loyalty and commitment to his land.
